intro:
This track answers two questions that every replicated system has to settle: what may a read return, and how do machines that crash and lose messages agree on anything? Lessons 1 and 2 make "consistent" precise. A consistency model is a rule about which values a read may return; you learn the ladder from linearizable down to eventual, how serializable differs from linearizable, what CAP and PACELC really say, and how to check a history for linearizability. Lesson 3 shows that a shared log, a compare-and-set register and one agreed value are the same problem, consensus, what the FLP result rules out, and how Paxos decides a value. Lesson 4 builds Raft. Lessons 5 and 6 are the products built on it: coordination services (ZooKeeper, etcd and Kafka's KRaft controllers) and distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB and Aurora DSQL). At the end you can name the model a setting buys, trace a Raft election and commit, build a leader election that a paused leader can't corrupt, and say what each distributed SQL design charges for its timestamps.

You need four earlier tracks: Replication (leaders, followers, lag and quorums), Partitioning (ranges and how requests find them), Transactions (isolation levels, MVCC and two-phase commit) and Faults, time and truth (partial failure, clocks, process pauses, fencing tokens and logical clocks). Each lesson reminds you of what it borrows.

The labs are plain Kotlin on a virtual clock, so a minute of elections, leases or clock skew runs in milliseconds, and the same seed always gives the same run; jqwik property tests throw hundreds of seeds at each one. Lessons 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 live in `labs/sim` (packages `sfz.cons.l01` to `l06`), and lesson 4's Raft lab lives in `labs/internals`. Run one from `labs/` with `./gradlew :sim:test --tests 'sfz.cons.l05.*'` (or `:internals:test` for lesson 4); the reference answers are in `src/solution`. None of the labs needs Docker. A few Try-its run real systems in Docker: a MongoDB replica set in lesson 1, ZooKeeper, etcd and a three-node KRaft cluster in lesson 5, and CockroachDB in lesson 6. Start one at a time and remove it when the Try it ends.
cheatsheet:
## Consistency models: what a read may return

| Model | Rule | Available on both sides of a partition? |
|---|---|---|
| Strict serializable | serializable, in an order that respects real time (Spanner: external consistency) | no |
| Linearizable | one object; each operation takes effect at one instant inside its call; once anyone reads a value, later reads can't go back | no |
| Sequential | one order that respects each process's own order, not real time | no |
| Causal | cause before effect, everywhere | sticky (stay with one replica) |
| Session guarantees | read your writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes follow reads | sticky |
| Eventual | replicas converge if writes stop (liveness only) | yes |
| Serializable | transactions as if one at a time, in some order; stale reads allowed | no |
| Snapshot isolation | reads from a snapshot, write-write conflicts abort; write skew allowed | no |

Linearizable is about one object and recency; serializable is about transactions and order. Neither implies the other.

CAP (Gilbert and Lynch): one register, linearizability, lost messages; during a partition a system gives up linearizability or availability. PACELC: else, it trades latency for consistency on every request (etcd: 0.7 ms linearizable against 0.3 ms serializable reads). Pick per request: Cassandra levels, DynamoDB `ConsistentRead`, MongoDB `readConcern`/`w`, PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit`, Kafka `acks`.

## Who gives linearizability

| Setup | Linearizable? |
|---|---|
| Single leader, all reads and writes on the real leader | yes, if the leader knows it is the leader |
| Consensus (Raft, Paxos) with ReadIndex or a lease for reads | yes |
| Leader reads without a leadership check | no: a deposed leader serves stale data |
| Multi-leader, leaderless quorums with w + r > n | no (quorum reads race); ABD read-repair fixes reads and writes, not compare-and-set |

Checking a history is NP-complete in general; check per key (locality). Tools: Knossos, Porcupine, Lincheck for JVM objects.

## Consensus

Agreement, integrity, validity (safety) and termination (liveness). Equivalent problems: consensus, linearizable compare-and-set, total order broadcast (a shared log), fault-tolerant atomic commit. FLP: no deterministic algorithm can guarantee termination in an asynchronous system with one crash, so real algorithms stay safe always and use timeouts to make progress.

| | Paxos | Raft |
|---|---|---|
| Epoch | ballot | term |
| Elect / prepare | prepare, promise (majority) | RequestVote (majority), only to an up-to-date log |
| Replicate | accept (majority); Multi-Paxos: one round trip per command | AppendEntries with prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm |
| Commit | value accepted by a majority under one ballot | entry of the current term on a majority (Figure 8) |
| Reads | leader with a lease or a quorum check | ReadIndex (heartbeat round) or a clock-based lease |
| Membership | (left to the implementer) | joint consensus, or one server at a time after the leader commits its no-op |

2f + 1 servers survive f failures: 3 survive 1, 5 survive 2, 4 still survive 1. Raft: random election timeouts (150 to 300 ms in the paper; etcd defaults to a 100 ms heartbeat and a 1,000 ms timeout); `broadcastTime ≪ electionTimeout ≪ MTBF`. Every vote and entry is on disk before the reply. More servers means slower writes (ZooKeeper: 21,000 writes a second on 3 servers, 8,000 on 13).

## Coordination services

| Primitive | ZooKeeper 3.9 | etcd 3.7 | Kafka 4 KRaft |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compare-and-set | `create` fails if it exists; versioned `setData` | `Txn` with comparisons | controller-checked metadata changes |
| Change counter | zxid, cZxid, cversion | cluster revision, create_revision, mod_revision | offset in `__cluster_metadata`, epochs |
| Failure detection | session; EPHEMERAL znodes | lease with a TTL; attached keys | broker heartbeats; fenced brokers |
| Notification | one-shot watches (persistent since 3.6) | watches from any kept revision | brokers fetch the metadata log |
| Reads | local, `sync` first for the latest | linearizable by default, serializable on request | brokers apply the log |

Recipes: leader election and locks (lowest sequence or create_revision wins; watch only your predecessor), service discovery (keys under a lease plus a watch; stale reads are fine), partition assignment (one key, compare-and-set on its revision). No lock gives mutual exclusion on its own: fence every write with the leader key's revision, checked by the resource in the same atomic step (Jepsen: about 18% lost updates with unfenced etcd locks and 2 s TTLs).

## Distributed SQL

Range sharding + a consensus group per range + two-phase commit with intents and a replicated transaction record + MVCC commit timestamps.

| System | Timestamps | Write pays | Read pays | Default isolation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TiDB | oracle (Placement Driver TSO) | oracle trips, 2PC over Raft | an oracle trip | snapshot (RR), pessimistic |
| FoundationDB | sequencer | a version, a resolver check (5 s limit) | a read version | strict serializable |
| Spanner | TrueTime [earliest, latest] | commit wait about 2ε (ε about 1 to 7 ms in 2012), overlapped with Paxos | may wait for safe time | serializable; REPEATABLE READ option |
| CockroachDB | hybrid logical clock, max offset 500 ms | one consensus round (parallel commits) | restart if a value falls in (T, T + max offset] | serializable; READ COMMITTED option |
| Aurora DSQL | adjudicators at commit | one adjudication, one journal write | nothing extra | snapshot only; 3,000 rows, 10 MiB, 5 min |

Retry SQLSTATE 40001 with an idempotency key, set the isolation level explicitly, and monitor clock offset.
recap: A consistency model is a rule about which values a read may return. Linearizable, sequential, causal, the session guarantees and eventual form a ladder; serializable and snapshot isolation are about transactions; strict serializable is both linearizable and serializable.

Nothing at or above sequential stays available on both sides of a partition (CAP), and even without one, stronger models cost latency on every request (PACELC). Products expose the choice per request, and their defaults are usually below linearizable.
Linearizability needs a leader that knows it leads, or consensus with checked reads. Quorums with w + r > n are not enough. Checking a history means searching for an order, per key.

Consensus, linearizable compare-and-set, total order broadcast and fault-tolerant atomic commit are one problem. FLP says no algorithm can promise to finish in a fully asynchronous system, so real ones stay safe always and use timeouts to make progress.

Paxos decides a value with two majority round trips; Multi-Paxos and Raft keep a stable leader and pay one round trip and an fsync per write. 2f + 1 servers survive f failures, and more servers make writes slower.

Raft: terms with at most one leader, votes only for up-to-date logs, AppendEntries' consistency check, commit by counting only current-term entries, ReadIndex or leases for reads, and one-server membership changes only after the new leader's no-op commits.

Coordination services (ZooKeeper, etcd, Kafka's KRaft controllers) give a few slow-changing facts four primitives: compare-and-set, a change counter, sessions with ephemeral keys, and watches. Elections, discovery and locks are recipes on top.
No lease or lock stops a paused holder: fence every write with a token from consensus (the leader key's revision), checked by the resource.

Distributed SQL stacks range sharding, Raft or Paxos per range, two-phase commit and MVCC timestamps. The timestamp source sets the guarantee and the bill: an oracle's round trip, Spanner's commit wait, CockroachDB's uncertainty restarts, or DSQL's optimistic snapshot isolation.

quiz.q: A banking app writes a new balance on the leader, then a follower that is 2 s behind serves the user's next page, which shows the old balance. Which guarantee is broken, and what is the cheapest fix?
options: Serializability; run every transaction at SERIALIZABLE
Read your writes; route that user's reads to the leader for a short while, or read at a position at least as new as their last write
Linearizability; replace the database with a consensus store
Eventual consistency; wait for the follower to converge
quiz.why: The user saw their own write disappear, which is the read-your-writes session guarantee. It only constrains one session, so tracking that session's last write position is enough; full linearizability would make every read pay for it. Serializability is about transactions and allows exactly this kind of stale read.

quiz.q: A Cassandra table uses QUORUM writes and QUORUM reads with a replication factor of 3, so every read set overlaps every write set. Is it linearizable?
options: Yes: w + r > n guarantees it
Only if all clocks are synchronized

No: a read concurrent with a write can return the new value from one replica while a later read returns the old value from two others; it needs read repair before returning (ABD), and compare-and-set needs consensus
Only for single-row tables
quiz.why: Overlap guarantees a read sees the latest completed write, not that two reads agree about a write still in progress. Once one reader has seen the new value, a later reader can still meet two replicas without it. Writing the value back to a quorum before returning closes that gap for reads and writes; a linearizable compare-and-set needs consensus, which is what Cassandra's lightweight transactions add.

quiz.q: Why can't any deterministic consensus algorithm promise to finish in a fully asynchronous system where one node may crash (FLP), and how does Raft live with that?
options: Messages can be corrupted; Raft uses checksums
Majorities can't overlap; Raft uses two-thirds quorums
Clocks drift; Raft uses atomic clocks
A slow node can't be told from a dead one, so the algorithm can be kept undecided forever; Raft never breaks safety and uses randomized timeouts so it decides whenever the network behaves for a while
quiz.why: FLP is about termination, not safety: an adversarial schedule can always delay the one message that would let the algorithm decide. Raft keeps its safety rules unconditional and only its progress depends on timing, through election timeouts, which is the partial synchrony real networks provide most of the time.

quiz.q: In single-decree Paxos, a proposer's prepare(5) gets promises from a majority, and one acceptor reports that it already accepted value "void" under ballot 3. The proposer wanted "capture". What must it send?
options: accept(5, "void"): it must adopt the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal it heard about
accept(5, "capture"): its own value, since it holds the higher ballot
Nothing: it must start again with ballot 6
accept(3, "void")
quiz.why: "void" may already be chosen by a majority that the proposer didn't hear from in full. Any majority overlaps that one, so the proposer saw at least one acceptor with "void", and the rule to adopt the highest-numbered accepted value keeps a chosen value chosen. Proposing its own value could choose a second value.

quiz.q: A new Raft leader for term 7 finds an entry from term 5 at index 40, stored on four of its five servers. When may it treat index 40 as committed?
options: At once: four of five is a majority
Only when all five store it
Once an entry from term 7 after it is stored on a majority; index 40 is committed along with it
Never: entries from old terms are discarded
quiz.why: Raft's Figure 8: a leader counts copies only for entries of its own term, because an old-term entry on a majority can still be overwritten by a server elected with a newer last term. Committing the leader's no-op (or any term-7 entry) on a majority commits every earlier entry through the Log Matching Property.

quiz.q: A Raft-based store's leader answers reads from memory. A partition isolates it, and the majority elects a new leader that commits a refund. A client then reads from the old leader. What should the old leader have done before answering?
options: Nothing; its log holds every committed entry
Confirm it still leads with a heartbeat round to a majority (ReadIndex), or rely on a lease that assumes bounded clock drift and no pauses
Forward the read to a random follower
Write the read into its log and wait for its own commit
quiz.why: Leader Completeness covers entries committed before its term, not after it was deposed. ReadIndex costs one round trip and no disk write; a lease costs none but trusts clocks. Writing the read into the log would also work but costs as much as a write, and an isolated leader could never commit it anyway.

quiz.q: Your service registers each instance in etcd under a lease and keeps a lock for its nightly payout job the same way. Which statement is right?
options: Discovery can use cached or serializable reads, since clients cope with dead endpoints anyway; the payout job's lock needs fencing, because a holder paused past its lease can still write
Both need linearizable reads and fencing
Neither needs fencing, because etcd uses Raft
Discovery needs fencing, and the lock doesn't
quiz.why: Discovery tolerates a list a second old: a client that dials a dead instance fails and retries. A lock guarding a payout is about correctness, and consensus inside etcd can't stop a paused process from writing to the payout store after its lease ends. The leader key's revision, checked by the store, does.

quiz.q: A ZooKeeper client crashes without closing its session. Its ephemeral znode marks it as the leader. What happens next?
options: The znode disappears the moment the TCP connection drops
The znode stays until an operator deletes it
Another client can delete it at once because it is ephemeral
The znode stays until the ensemble expires the session after its timeout with no heartbeat; then it is deleted and the next candidate's watch fires
quiz.why: The ensemble, not the client, decides when a session is dead, and only after the negotiated timeout (2 to 20 times tickTime). Until then the crashed client still looks like the leader, which is why takeover takes about one session timeout, and why the timeout is a trade between fast failover and false alarms during GC pauses.

quiz.q: Spanner and CockroachDB both make a transaction's timestamp respect real time, yet only one of them makes every write wait. Why?
options: CockroachDB doesn't replicate writes

Spanner's clocks have a small, known error (TrueTime), so waiting it out on each commit is cheap; CockroachDB's bound on ordinary clocks is large (500 ms by default), so it makes readers that meet an uncertain value restart instead
Spanner uses an oracle
CockroachDB only runs in one region
quiz.why: Commit wait costs about twice the clock error on every write, a few milliseconds with TrueTime but far too much with a 500 ms bound. CockroachDB moves the cost to reads of recently written keys, which happen less often. Neither uses an oracle; TiDB does.

quiz.q: A team ports a scheduling service that relied on Oracle's serializable isolation for a "no doctor goes off call alone" rule to Aurora DSQL. What should they expect?
options: Exactly the same behaviour: DSQL is distributed SQL, so it is serializable
Deadlocks under load
Write skew: DSQL offers only snapshot isolation, which checks write-write conflicts; they need a shared row both transactions write, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which DSQL adjudicates as a write
Lost updates on single rows
quiz.why: Two transactions that each read both doctors and update a different one don't conflict under snapshot isolation, so both commit. DSQL has no deadlocks, since nothing waits on locks, and it does catch two writes to the same row. Note also that Oracle's own SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, so the rule may never have been safe there either.
